attribution.author: Paul McWhorter
attribution.note: Lesson curriculum based on Paul McWhorter's Arduino tutorial series at toptechboy.com. Please support his free educational work on Patreon.

tracks.name: Arduino Electronics
tracks.blurb: Build real circuits and write the C++ that drives them — LEDs, sensors, servos, motors, and displays.

tracks.name: Build on Your Computer
tracks.blurb: Leave the sandbox: set up your own machine. The command line, git, compilers, and running real projects — typed, not clicked.

tracks.name: Arduino Nano & Motion
tracks.blurb: Point it, spin it, balance it. The Arduino Nano with a 9-axis IMU — accelerometers, gyros, sensor fusion, and PID control.

tracks.name: Raspberry Pi & Linux
tracks.blurb: A whole Linux computer for the price of a sensor. Master the Pi's command line, then drive its GPIO pins with Python.

tracks.name: Python & Data
tracks.blurb: Bring your circuits into Python — a virtual 3D world, live data plots, and boards talking to each other over the network.

tracks.name: AI on the Edge
tracks.blurb: Give a Raspberry Pi eyes: py5 and OpenCV for vision, MediaPipe for hands and gestures, and neural nets running on-device.

tracks.name: Compute Hardware — CPU · GPU · NPU
tracks.blurb: Open the black box. How a CPU runs your instructions one by one, how a GPU does thousands at once, and what an NPU adds for AI.

lessons.title: Digital Output — LED Blink
lessons.description: Control a digital pin and blink an LED using pinMode() and digitalWrite(). Build the circuit: pin 13 → resistor → LED → GND.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino Tutorials 1–2 — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Wire pin 13 to one side of the resistor, the other side to the LED anode (A), and the LED cathode (C) to GND.

lessons.title: Analog Input — Potentiometer
lessons.description: Read a potentiometer, map its value, and print to the serial monitor. Wire the pot: VCC→5V, GND→GND, SIG→A0.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino Tutorial 10 — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: The wiper (SIG) picks off a voltage between 0V and 5V. Wire it to analog pin A0.

lessons.title: Serial Monitor — Talking to Your Arduino
lessons.description: Use Serial.begin(), Serial.print(), and Serial.println() to send readable data to your computer. No external circuit needed.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino serial tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: No external parts — the serial monitor communicates over the USB cable.

lessons.title: Variables — Making Code Adjustable
lessons.description: Replace magic numbers with named int variables so one edit changes the whole sketch. Same LED circuit as Lesson 1.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino Tutorial 4 (Variables) — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Rebuild the Lesson 1 circuit: pin → resistor → LED anode, cathode → GND.

lessons.title: Conditionals — Making Decisions
lessons.description: Use if/else to switch the LED based on the potentiometer: turn it past halfway and the light comes on.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino if-statement tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Two sub-circuits: the pot (VCC/GND/SIG→A0) for input, and pin 13 → resistor → LED → GND for output.

lessons.title: Digital Input — Pushbutton
lessons.description: Read a pushbutton with INPUT_PULLUP and light the LED while it's held. Remember: with a pullup, pressed reads LOW.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino button tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Button between pin 2 and GND (INPUT_PULLUP handles the rest internally). LED circuit on pin 13 as usual.

lessons.title: Debouncing — Clean Button Presses
lessons.description: Metal contacts bounce. Use millis() to ignore changes for 50ms so one press counts exactly once — toggle the LED per press.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino debounce tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Same wiring as Lesson 6: button on pin 2 to GND, LED circuit on pin 13.

lessons.title: Light Sensor — Photoresistor
lessons.description: Read the light level with a photoresistor module and print it to the serial monitor. Cover the sensor and watch the numbers fall.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino photoresistor tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Module wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, AO→A0. The AO voltage rises with brightness.

lessons.title: Night Light — Light + LED
lessons.description: Combine sensing and output: when it gets dark, the LED turns on automatically — a real night light.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino light-meter tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Photoresistor module AO→A0, plus the LED circuit on pin 13.

lessons.title: Temperature — NTC Thermistor
lessons.description: Read temperature with an NTC thermistor module and print approximate °C using map().
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino thermistor tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Module wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, OUT→A0.

lessons.title: Ultrasonic Distance — HC-SR04
lessons.description: Measure distance like a bat: ping with TRIG, time the echo with pulseIn(), and convert microseconds to centimeters.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino HC-SR04 tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, TRIG→pin 9, ECHO→pin 10.

lessons.title: Distance Alarm — Sonar + LED
lessons.description: The capstone: when something comes closer than 20cm, the warning LED lights — a parking sensor.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino distance-alarm tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: HC-SR04 wiring (TRIG→9, ECHO→10) plus the LED circuit on pin 13.

lessons.title: PWM — Dimming an LED
lessons.description: analogWrite() pulses a pin faster than the eye can see — the duty cycle becomes brightness. Fade the LED up and down with for loops.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino analogWrite/PWM tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Same LED circuit, but on a PWM pin: pin 9 (~) → resistor → LED anode, cathode → GND.

lessons.title: RGB LED — Mixing Colors
lessons.description: Three PWM channels, 16.7 million colors. Drive the red, green, and blue legs with analogWrite() and mix your own color.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino RGB LED tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: COM (longest leg) → GND. R leg → pin 9, G leg → pin 10, B leg → pin 11 (all PWM ~). Real builds put a 220Ω on each leg.

lessons.title: Servo — Sweep
lessons.description: A servo moves to the exact angle you command. Include the Servo library, attach pin 9, and sweep the horn from 0° to 180° and back.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino servo tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Servo wiring: GND → GND, V+ → 5V, PWM (signal) → pin 9.

lessons.title: Servo + Potentiometer — Steering
lessons.description: Close the loop with your own hand: map the pot's 0–1023 onto 0–180° and the servo horn follows the knob.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino servo knob tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Servo: GND→GND, V+→5V, PWM→pin 9. Pot: VCC→5V, GND→GND, SIG→A0.

lessons.title: DC Motor — Fan Speed
lessons.description: PWM sets the motor's average voltage, and average voltage is speed. The pot becomes a fan-speed dial.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino DC motor tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Motor: terminal 1 → pin 9 (~), terminal 2 → GND. Pot: VCC→5V, GND→GND, SIG→A0. (Real builds add a transistor driver + flyback diode.)

lessons.title: LCD — Hello, World!
lessons.description: Ten wires and your project can talk. Wire the 16×2 display and print text plus a live seconds counter.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino LCD tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Power: VSS→GND, VDD→5V, V0→GND, RW→GND, A→5V, K→GND. Signals: RS→12, E→11, D4→5, D5→4, D6→3, D7→2.

lessons.title: LCD Thermometer
lessons.description: Combine the temp sensor with the display: a self-contained instrument that shows °C with no computer attached.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino LCD + sensor tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: LCD wired as in Lesson 18 (RS→12, E→11, D4→5, D5→4, D6→3, D7→2). Temp sensor: VCC→5V, GND→GND, OUT→A0.

lessons.title: Capstone — Parking Radar
lessons.description: Everything at once: sonar measures distance, the LCD reports it, and the RGB LED glows green → amber → red as you get close.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino capstone-style projects — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Sonar: TRIG→8, ECHO→10. LCD: RS→12, E→11, D4→7, D5→6, D6→4, D7→2. RGB: R leg→3, G leg→5, COM→GND.

lessons.title: Piezo Buzzer — First Beep
lessons.description: Give your projects a voice. One new part, two commands: tone() picks a pitch and noTone() cuts it. Build a little two-note alarm you can hear.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino tone()/buzzer tutorials — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Buzzer: + terminal (pin 1) → Arduino pin 8. – terminal (pin 2) → GND. A piezo buzzer needs no resistor and no pinMode — tone() drives the pin for you.

lessons.title: Reverse Parking Beeper
lessons.description: Keep the sonar from the radar build and add the buzzer: the closer an object gets, the higher and faster it beeps — exactly like a car's reverse sensor. Under 10 cm it holds a solid warning tone.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino sonar + buzzer projects — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: Sonar: VCC→5V, GND→GND, TRIG→8, ECHO→10. Buzzer: + (pin 1) → pin 9, – (pin 2) → GND. Drag the distance slider while it runs to hear the pitch change.

lessons.title: Weather Station
lessons.description: Keep the LCD from the thermometer build and add a DHT11 — a single sensor that reads BOTH temperature and humidity over one data wire. A library decodes the sensor for you; you just call readTemperature() and readHumidity() and print them to the display. Drag the Temp and Humidity sliders while it runs to watch the readout change.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino DHT11 + LCD projects — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: LCD wired as in Lesson 19 (RS→12, E→11, D4→5, D5→4, D6→3, D7→2; VSS/V0/RW/K→GND, VDD/A→5V). DHT11: VCC→5V, GND→GND, SDA (data)→7. The DHT object in the code uses pin 7.

lessons.title: Remote Control
lessons.description: Keep the 16×2 LCD and add an infrared receiver so your project can take orders from a TV-style remote. A library decodes the invisible pulses for you: each time a key arrives you read its command byte and print it to the screen. Run the sketch, then click keys on the remote to watch their codes appear — power is 162, the number keys each have their own value.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino IR remote lessons — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: LCD wired as in Lesson 19 (RS→12, E→11, D4→5, D5→4, D6→3, D7→2; VSS/V0/RW/K→GND, VDD/A→5V). IR receiver: VCC→5V, GND→GND, DAT→7 (matches IR_RECEIVE_PIN in the code). Drop the remote on the canvas — it needs no wires, it beams infrared through the air.

lessons.title: Stepper Motor
lessons.description: Keep the 16×2 LCD and add a stepper motor — a motor that turns in exact, countable steps instead of just spinning. The Stepper library does the coil-switching for you: set a speed in RPM, then command whole revolutions forward and back while the LCD announces each move. Run the sketch and watch the shaft's arrow sweep one full turn one way, then the other. This is the same kind of motor that positions a 3D-printer head.
lessons.source: Paul McWhorter, Arduino stepper motor lessons — toptechboy.com

circuit.notes: LCD wired as in Lesson 19 (RS→12, E→11, D4→5, D5→4, D6→3, D7→2; VSS/V0/RW/K→GND, VDD/A→5V). Stepper coils: A−→6, A+→7, B+→8, B−→9 — the same four pins, in the same order, that you pass to Stepper myStepper(steps, 6, 7, 8, 9). A real stepper would need a ULN2003 driver board between the Uno and the coils; the simulator drives it directly.

lessons.title: Meet the Command Line
lessons.description: The terminal lets you drive your computer with words instead of clicks — the way every professional developer works. Type each command, press Enter, and watch the machine respond. Same 'type it, see it' loop as the Arduino track, now for your own PC.
lessons.source: Synapsys Dev-Setup track

terminal.intro: This is a safe practice terminal. Nothing here touches your real computer, but every command behaves exactly like the real thing. Work down the checklist on the right — type each command yourself.

steps.why: Print Working Directory — asks the shell 'where am I right now?' It answers with your current folder's path.
List the files and folders in the current directory. Right now it's empty, so nothing prints.
MaKe DIRectory — create a new folder named hello-cli.
List again. Now you can see the hello-cli folder you just made.
Change Directory — step inside the folder.
Confirm you moved. The path now ends in /hello-cli.

lessons.title: Files & Folders
lessons.description: Creating, reading, and organising files from the keyboard. These four commands — echo, cat, touch, mkdir — are the bread and butter of working in a project folder.
lessons.source: Synapsys Dev-Setup track

terminal.intro: You're inside the hello-cli folder from the last lesson. Let's put some files in it. The > symbol means 'send this output into a file' instead of printing it to the screen.

steps.why: echo prints text; > redirects that text into a new file called notes.txt.
List the folder — notes.txt now exists.
conCATenate — dump a file's contents to the screen. You'll see your saved line.
Make a src folder to hold source code — a very common project layout.
touch creates an empty file. Here it makes app.js inside src/.
Show the folder as a tree so you can see the whole structure at a glance.

lessons.title: Git — Version Control
lessons.description: Git is the time machine every developer relies on: it snapshots your project so you can never truly lose work. Here you'll turn a folder into a Git repository and record your first commit.
lessons.source: Synapsys Dev-Setup track

terminal.intro: A 'repository' is a folder Git is watching. You initialise it once, then 'stage' the files you want to save and 'commit' them as a permanent snapshot.

steps.why: Check that Git is installed and see which version you have.
Turn this folder into a Git repository — it creates a hidden .git folder to store history.
Ask Git what it sees: which files are new, changed, or already saved.
Stage every file (the . means 'everything here') — mark it to be included in the next snapshot.
Save a permanent snapshot. The -m message describes what this snapshot is.
View the history. Your first commit is now recorded forever.

lessons.title: Your First Real Program
lessons.description: Bring it all together: use a compiler toolchain (.NET) to scaffold, then build and run a genuine program from the command line — the exact workflow you'd use on a real project.
lessons.source: Synapsys Dev-Setup track

terminal.intro: A compiler turns human-readable code into a program your machine can run. The dotnet tool scaffolds a starter project, then builds and runs it for you.

steps.why: Confirm the .NET compiler toolchain is installed.
Scaffold a new console app named hello — it writes Program.cs and a project file for you.
Step into the project folder that was just created.
See what the template made: Program.cs (your code) and hello.csproj (the project settings).
Read the starter code — a single line that prints Hello, World!.
Compile and run the program. 'Hello, World!' is your machine running code you built.
